notes.b: Dehydration (drying) removes most of the water from food. Micro-organisms and enzymes both need water to work, so taking it away keeps the food from spoiling.
points: Micro-organisms need available water to grow. With most of the water removed, they cannot multiply, and enzymes (the natural chemicals in food that cause ripening and decay) cannot act either.
Drying to a low moisture level stops micro-organisms growing but does not kill all of them. They are only inactivated, so they can grow again if the food takes in moisture.
Fresh fruit and vegetables contain roughly 70 to 95 per cent water, so they lose most of their weight when dried and become much lighter and smaller.
Dried food is light and compact, which reduces its storage space and the cost of transporting it.
Damp dried food can re-absorb moisture from the air and go mouldy, so it must be stored dry and airtight.

Blanching vegetables (dipping them briefly in boiling water) before drying inactivates enzymes that would otherwise cause darkening and off-flavours during storage. Fruit is treated differently: it is dipped in lemon juice or an ascorbic acid solution, or sulphured, to stop browning.
notes.tip: Always say micro-organisms cannot grow because water is unavailable. Drying does not kill them, so rehydrated or damp dried food can spoil. Dehydration here means removing water from food, not the lack of water in the body.

notes.b: Home drying uses gentle heat and moving air to carry moisture away from thin pieces of food. The methods differ in how much control you have over temperature and drying time.
points: Preparation: choose ripe, sound, undamaged produce and wash it thoroughly. Cut it into even, thin pieces so that they all dry at the same rate, blanch vegetables, and arrange the pieces in a single layer.
Oven drying: food is spread in a single layer on trays and dried at a very low temperature, with the oven door slightly open so moisture can escape. It takes several hours.
Electric dehydrator: a fan circulates warm air at a controlled low temperature over trays, so food dries evenly and reliably.

Sun drying: food is laid on trays or racks in strong, dry heat. It is slow and depends on the weather, and exposes food to dust, insects and moisture, so it suits hot, dry countries rather than the damp Irish climate.
Sun drying is common for fruit in hot countries, such as raisins, apricots and sun-dried tomatoes.
Air drying: herbs are tied in small bunches and hung in a warm, dry, airy place away from direct sunlight, which would fade them. Beans and pulses can also be left to dry on the plant.
notes.tip: If asked to name a method for a surplus of home-grown produce, give the method, the principle (water removed so micro-organisms cannot grow) and the steps: select, wash, cut thinly, blanch vegetables, dry in a single layer.

notes.h: Testing, conditioning and storing dried food
notes.b: Food that looks dry may still hold pockets of moisture, and moisture is what lets mould return. So dried food is tested, conditioned and then packed carefully.
points: Test dryness: dried fruit should be leathery and pliable, with no moist centre or sticky patches, which would let micro-organisms grow.
Dried vegetables should be brittle and snap cleanly when bent.
Condition dried food by packing it loosely in a jar for several days and shaking the jar daily. Condensation on the inside of the jar means the food needs more drying.
Store dried food in airtight, moisture-proof containers in a cool, dark, dry place, since light and moisture reduce its quality and damp lets mould grow.

notes.b: Many foods dry well, especially those that are mostly water and have a flavour that survives the process.
points: Fruit such as apples, apricots, pears, bananas and grapes (which become raisins).
Vegetables such as onions, carrots, tomatoes, peas and beans.
Herbs such as mint, parsley, thyme and rosemary, which keep their flavour well when dried.
Pulses and cereals, which are naturally dry foods that keep well.
Meat and fish, which are salted before drying or smoked and dried, as in stockfish (dried fish) and jerky (dried strips of meat).
notes.tip: For short questions on drying as a method, good examples are carrots, tomatoes and onions, fruit and vegetables, and meat and fish.

notes.b: Factories dry food on a large scale, often by turning liquid foods into powders or flakes. The most advanced method, accelerated freeze drying, gives the best quality but costs the most. Freeze-dried foods keep their shape, colour and flavour better than air-dried foods.
points: Spray drying: liquid food such as milk, coffee, eggs or soup is sprayed as a fine mist into a stream of hot air. The water evaporates in seconds and the powder falls. It is used for milk powder, instant coffee and infant formula.
Drum (roller) drying: a thin layer of liquid or purée is spread on a heated rotating drum, dries, and is scraped off as flakes. It is used for potato flakes (instant mashed potato) and baby cereals.
Tunnel or cabinet drying: trays or a conveyor belt of food pass through a tunnel of hot air. It is used for fruit and vegetables.

Accelerated freeze drying (AFD): 1. The food is frozen quickly. 2. It is placed in a vacuum chamber and gently heated. 3. The ice turns directly into water vapour without melting, a change called sublimation, and the vapour is drawn off.
4. This leaves a dry, porous food that keeps its shape.
AFD food is packed airtight, often with nitrogen, and is used for coffee, fruit pieces, vegetables in instant soups, camping and ready meals, and herbs.

AFD is valued because the food keeps its colour, flavour, shape and nutrients well (little heat is used, and no liquid water moves to the surface). It rehydrates quickly and fully, is very light, and has a long shelf life.
AFD is limited because the equipment and energy are expensive, so the food costs more.
Diagram: draw AFD in three labelled stages: frozen food; vacuum chamber with ice changing to vapour (sublimation); condenser and dry product.
notes.tip: Freezing is only the first step of freeze drying, and it is not the same as freezing as a preservation method. Say the ice turns directly into vapour: sublimation is not melting or evaporation. Higher Level questions can ask you to describe AFD.

notes.b: Drying keeps food safe for a long time, but heat and the loss of water change its nutrients, appearance and texture. These effects are examined, usually with fruit and vegetables.
points: Water-soluble vitamins, especially vitamin C and the B vitamins, are lost during drying.
Vitamins A and E are reduced, because they are sensitive to heat and oxidation.
Colour darkens or fades, especially in fruit left in the sun, because of oxidation and browning reactions. Vegetables are blanched, and fruit is dipped in lemon juice, to reduce this.
Dried fruit is concentrated in sugar, so a small portion gives much more sugar and energy than the same weight of fresh fruit. Sticky dried fruit can also cause dental decay.
Texture becomes leathery, chewy or brittle, and the flavour becomes more concentrated. Dried food also shrinks and wrinkles.
Minerals and fibre are not destroyed by drying, and protein and carbohydrate are also kept.
Most dried foods must be soaked or cooked in water (rehydrated) before use. Spray-dried and freeze-dried foods rehydrate easily, and the soaking water contains vitamins and can be used.
Advantages: long shelf life without refrigeration, light and compact, no freezer needed, cheap to transport and store, and concentrated flavour.
Disadvantages: vitamin loss, changed colour and texture, slow, needs correct storage, some foods do not rehydrate well, and high sugar in dried fruit.
notes.tip: For effects of dehydration, name vitamins by group: C and B are lost, A and E are reduced. Also give the change in colour, texture and flavour, the prevention of microbial and enzyme activity, and the high sugar in dried fruit. Two or three effects score 3 marks.

keyTerms.definition: Removing most of the water from food so that micro-organisms and enzymes cannot grow or act.
The water in food that is free to be used by micro-organisms and enzymes, as opposed to water bound to other food components.
A commercial drying method in which food is frozen and then the ice is removed under vacuum by sublimation.
The change of a solid directly into a gas without first becoming a liquid, as occurs with ice in freeze drying.
Drying a liquid by spraying it as a mist into hot air so that the water evaporates in seconds, leaving a powder.
Drying a thin layer of liquid or purée on a heated rotating drum to produce flakes.
Storing dried food in a loosely filled jar for several days so that residual moisture is evenly distributed and any remaining dampness shows as condensation.
Soaking dried food in water so that it absorbs moisture and returns towards its fresh texture before cooking.

factCards.definition: Oven drying, electric dehydrator drying and sun drying (used in hot, dry countries).
Vitamin C, the B vitamins, vitamin A and vitamin E.
The food is frozen, placed in a vacuum chamber, and the ice sublimes directly to water vapour, leaving a dry, porous structure.
It is leathery and pliable, with no moist centre or sticky patches.

factCards.term: Sign that dried food needs more drying
factCards.definition: Condensation inside the jar during conditioning.

questions.prompt: Explain why micro-organisms cannot grow in properly dried food, and state one effect that drying has on the vitamin content of food.
questions.model: Micro-organisms need available water to grow and reproduce; removing most of the water from food makes it unavailable, so growth stops, although micro-organisms are not necessarily killed. Drying also reduces the enzyme activity that would cause spoilage. One effect on vitamins: water-soluble vitamins such as vitamin C and the B vitamins are lost during drying, and vitamins A and E are reduced by heat and oxidation.

questions.prompt: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of drying fruit and vegetables at home compared with freezing them.
questions.model: Advantages of drying: food is light and compact and needs no freezer, so it is convenient for storage and for an unplugged or power-cut situation; dried foods keep for a long period when stored dry and airtight; concentrated flavour and sugar make dried fruit useful as a snack or ingredient. Disadvantages: vitamin C and B vitamins are lost more than in freezing; colour darkens and texture changes; dried fruit is high in sugar per portion; drying takes many hours and the process must be controlled to avoid mould. Freezing keeps colour, texture and nutrients better but needs a freezer and continuous energy. Each point is set against the matching point for freezing.
